Each dot is one historical 20-year T-bill roll, plotted by how many times it multiplied the money, with the guaranteed x2 marked as a vertical line.

A running figure of "52.3% overall" appears, meaning 52.3% of T-bill rolls beat x2. The last frames split the history into three eras: 1934-1949 (0.0% beat x2), 1950-1989 (93.1% beat x2) and 1990-2006 (5.0% beat x2).

3. It means that rolling T-bills for 20 years has not reliably beaten a guaranteed doubling. It beat it only about half the time overall, and the result depended heavily on when you started. Outcomes were close to all-or-nothing by era: almost never in the low-rate periods, and almost always in the high-inflation, high-rate era. The caption "Not a pick. What history did." says these are the actual historical results, not a cherry-picked scenario.

4. A viewer in their 40s with money they will not need for 20 years would take away that T-bills or cash are not a safe path to a particular outcome. They are a gamble on which interest-rate era you land in, and a guaranteed x2 over 20 years (about 3.5% a year) would have been a coin flip to beat. So a locked-in guaranteed return, such as a long-term bond or similar product, is worth comparing against rolling short-term bills, rather than assuming that waiting in bills is automatically better. The video does not say what to buy, only that the choice should not rest on the assumption that rolling bills will do well.
